hits.text:
Next question: why are you still using branches?

We talked about PRs. I don't think they make sense anymore, if you rethink them from first principles.

Yes, if you only use them to trigger CI, then sure, go ahead. That's a fat commit, not a PR. But for mandatory code review? Knowledge sharing? C'mon.

But some of you said: "we use PRs because we use branches! I love to keep my stuff on branches."

And I'm here to tell you: you don't need branches! You can just push to main.

It's called trunk-based development and the idea behind it is true continuous integration: you continuously integrate your changes with the trunk, the main branch.

It's been around for a while, it works. Just yesterday I talked with someone who said they've used it in an org with 400 engineers, without any issues. Ruby, the project, uses trunk-based development.

The main idea is that you want to avoid long-lived branches. They're bad, because branches can diverge and merging can turn into a thing. And you don't want routine operations to become a thing.

Even when I worked in teams that used PRs and branches, I considered it a smell when a branch lived for longer than a day or two.

But when I shared this with others, I'd often get something back like this:

"Well, good for you, but no. MY thing, what I'm working on, that can't be done on main. It needs to be on a branch! It has a database migration, it changes the underlying shape, the architecture, it refactors this and changes that. It can't go on main yet! I need to merge it all at the end."

And then I'd say:

"Nah, I can merge nearly anything continuously in small commits to main. You split things up. Add the column first, merge that, deploy it, now it's out, works, safe.

Add the helpers first, merge them, get them out.

Want to migrate from legacy pattern A to new pattern B? Don't do it all at once. Add the dependency, then migrate A to B, one by one, safe."

If it can be merged in a large change, I bet it can be done in small increments that you merge to main.

Yes, there are exceptions, but it's 0.5% of cases, not 50%.

But there was a real problem with this approach: it was hard!

There's a lot of "meta programming" you have to do: make sure this small first change compiles and runs and the tests work, merge it, get it out, monitor it; then do the next small piece, make sure that works and get it out; then maybe push some still-unused dead code, add a feature flag, add a config variable; or keep both configurations working at the same time, etc.

That meant sometimes it was just easier to do it in a big fat branch. But big fat branches are risky!

A system that continuously flows is safer than a system that starts and stops in spurts.

But -- you guessed it -- here's the good news:

Now, with agents, all of these chores are no chores at all!

Agents are great at adding feature flags, they're great at splitting up code, they're great at keeping track of three changes and merging them one by one and watching them roll out. They're great at keeping two configurations working for a day. They're great at migrating one by one.

In other words: it's now 10x easier to just work on main and make sure everything is continuously integrated and working.

It's now easy to make sure the system constantly flows.

And look, ...

I'm not here to convince you to switch to trunk-based development. Just a ruse to get you to read this. (But also, hey: try it! Pushing to main is amazing.)

I'm here to make you RETHINK how you develop software.

Don't just use agents to replace your typing.

Use agents as the magic code-writing machines they are. Everything that was hard about software development because it involved writing code -- even the meta programming -- has become easier.

You can now reach for the stars! But you need to look up.

hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Prefix-aware LLM routing, clearly explained!

(trick to get first LLM token 170x sooner)

Production prompts start with the same system prompt, tool definitions and earlier turns, and only the last part of each request is new.

So the GPU that served the previous turn still holds the KV cache for that shared prefix, but a cache-blind router may send the next request to a different GPU, which then has to recompute the whole prefix before it can write a single token.

A prefix-aware router avoids this by tracking which GPU holds which part of each prompt.

The visual below shows how it works:

↳ When a request arrives with prefix blocks A to D and a new suffix E, the router hashes the prompt block by block, so each hash covers everything before it.

↳ It looks those hashes up in a block-to-worker index, which stores locations and never the KV tensors themselves.

↳ Worker A holds 2 matching blocks, Worker C holds 3 and Worker B holds all 4, so Worker B gets the request.

↳ Worker B reuses the cached KV for A to D, computes KV only for E, and starts decoding.

↳ Once E is cached, a cache event updates the router's index, so the next turn lands on Worker B too.

If no worker has a match, the request gets a full prefill on whichever worker the router picks.

In a popular benchmark on 8 vLLM pods across 16 H100s, prefix-aware routing brought p90 time to first token down to 0.54s, while random routing took 92.5s on the same pods.

Real routers also weigh load alongside cache matches, so the GPU with the warmest cache doesn't end up with the longest queue.

All of this depends on the prefix cache itself working, and a small change early in the prompt can make every block after it miss.

I covered how prefix caching works, and how prompt changes cause cache miss, in a detailed article.

Read it below.

virals.text:
GitHub has released Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot, which orchestrates between Anthropic and OpenAI models. It scores 2 points below Opus 5.5 in Claude Code at half the Cost per Task in the Coding Agent Index

GitHub describes Copilot Fusion as a runtime orchestration system, which selects and coordinates models to optimize performance, cost, and latency for each task. Copilot Fusion chooses between a number of models from Anthropic and OpenAI, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6 Sol. We benchmarked its max setting in GitHub Copilot CLI in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0.

Token costs are charged based on the underlying models used to complete a request.

Key takeaways:

➤ Cost-efficient for near-frontier performance: Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot costs $5.59 per task, versus $11.42 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max). Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) scores 62 at $8.00 per task.

➤ Slight lead in Terminal-Bench 4.0: The Coding Agent Index v2.0 weights its three constituent benchmarks equally. Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with a score of 71. It ranks third on FrontierCode in the chart at 51, behind Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max) at 56 and Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) at 54. Its SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA score lags at 57, between GPT-6 Astra in Codex and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity CLI.

➤ Half the token use of Opus 5.5 in Claude Code: GitHub Copilot Fusion used 7.2M tokens per task in the Coding Agent Index, approximately half of the tokens used by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, and 30% less than Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high).

outsiders.name: Artificial Analysis
outsiders.text:
GitHub has released Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot, which orchestrates between Anthropic and OpenAI models. It scores 2 points below Opus 5.5 in Claude Code at half the Cost per Task in the Coding Agent Index

GitHub describes Copilot Fusion as a runtime orchestration system, which selects and coordinates models to optimize performance, cost, and latency for each task. Copilot Fusion chooses between a number of models from Anthropic and OpenAI, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6 Sol. We benchmarked its max setting in GitHub Copilot CLI in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0.

Token costs are charged based on the underlying models used to complete a request.

Key takeaways:

➤ Cost-efficient for near-frontier performance: Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot costs $5.59 per task, versus $11.42 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max). Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) scores 62 at $8.00 per task.

➤ Slight lead in Terminal-Bench 4.0: The Coding Agent Index v2.0 weights its three constituent benchmarks equally. Copilot Fusion in GitHub Copilot leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with a score of 71. It ranks third on FrontierCode in the chart at 51, behind Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max) at 56 and Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high) at 54. Its SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA score lags at 57, between GPT-6 Astra in Codex and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity CLI.

➤ Half the token use of Opus 5.5 in Claude Code: GitHub Copilot Fusion used 7.2M tokens per task in the Coding Agent Index, approximately half of the tokens used by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, and 30% less than Devin Fusion with Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high).

outsiders.text:
Radar is back on Product Hunt today!

In May we launched it as an open-source Kubernetes UI, focused on humans - finally giving engineers everywhere an actually nice UI for Kubernetes. Now at 4k stars, people seemed to like it :)

AI agents also deserve better.

A lot of teams are trying to figure out if they need an AI SRE, which one, how to integrate it. Turns out, you have a pretty good one already - whichever agent you're already using, Claude Code, Codex or anything else. 
The missing part is better cluster context and tools, not a fancier agent.

We tested plain Claude Code with Radar MCP against 5 AI SRE tools on 50 benchmarks - with Radar it got the most right, the fastest and the cheapest by far. With Radar Cloud, you can also have it automatically detect issues and send you full investigation to Slack before you even realized something was broken.

If you run Kubernetes, I'd love your take: 
https://t.co/EKQm0CyedL

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
